title: Getting started with deaviz
text: deaviz ships chinese_cities, classic cross-sectional DEA benchmark 35 cities three inputs three outputs (Sueyoshi, 1992). dea_data() records columns inputs, outputs, identifies DMU. Columns can given name position. dea_data object can defined either input output variable names follows: equivalently location : Everything downstream takes d object. input/output columns prefixed i_ / o_, dea_data() detects automatically can skip inputs/outputs arguments.
code: d <- dea_data(   chinese_cities,   inputs  = c("industrial_labour_force", "working_funds", "investments"),   outputs = c("gross_industrial_output", "profit_and_tax", "retail_sales"),   id      = "DMU" ) d #> <dea_data> #>   DMUs    : 35 #>   Inputs  : 3 (industrial_labour_force, working_funds, investments) #>   Outputs : 3 (gross_industrial_output, profit_and_tax, retail_sales) d <- dea_data(   chinese_cities,   inputs  = 2:4,   outputs = 5:7,   id      = "DMU" )

title: Getting started with deaviz
text: compute_efficiency() returns radial efficiency scores (plus peer weights multiplier weights). Returns--scale orientation arguments.
code: eff <- compute_efficiency(x = d, rts = "vrs", orientation = "in") head(round(eff$eff, 3)) #> [1] 1.000 0.944 0.805 0.779 0.875 0.686

title: Getting started with deaviz
text: Start looking spread. plot_efficiency_distributions() shows distribution efficiency scores, plot_io_distributions() shows raw input/output variables.   Note x_angle = 30: input/output names long, tilting x-axis tick labels keeps readable. Every plot whose x-axis carries variable DMU names accepts x_angle. plot_io_efficients() counts many DMUs efficient versus inefficient.
code: plot_efficiency_distributions(d, rts = "vrs", title = "Chinese Cities Efficiency Scores", subtitle = "Variable Return To Scale") plot_io_distributions(d, type = "box", x_angle = 30) plot_io_efficients(d, rts = "vrs", transparency = 1)

text: Two ways project multidimensional input/output space onto readable plane. plot_io_pca_biplot() uses PCA, drawing input/output loading vectors; plot_io_mds() uses metric (ratio) multidimensional scaling via smacof majorization algorithm (de Leeuw & Mair, 2009). graphical use projections DEA follows Adler & Raveh (2008). title: Getting started with deaviz
text: Cross-efficiency scores every DMU using every DMU’s optimal weights (Doyle & Green, 1994). compute_cross_efficiency() builds matrix, plot_cem_heatmap() displays. plot_cem_unfolding() unfolds matrix map rates favourably (Ashkiani & Mar-Molinero, 2017), plot_cem_weights_heatmap() shows underlying weight profiles.    want highlight specific DMU? , can use labels= argument:
code: cem <- compute_cross_efficiency(d)  plot_cem_heatmap(cem, x_angle = 90) plot_cem_unfolding(cem) plot_cem_weights_heatmap(d, x_angle = 30) plot_cem_weights_heatmap(d, x_angle = 30, labels = "Xian")

text: plot_io_radar() plot_io_parcoo() show DMU’s full input/output profile, radar polygon parallel-coordinates line.   accept variables argument show subset profile: "" (default), "inputs", "outputs", vector variable names positions.
code: plot_io_radar(d, efficiency = "vrs") plot_io_parcoo(d, efficiency = "vrs", x_angle = 30) plot_io_parcoo(d, variables = "inputs", efficiency = "vrs", x_angle = 30)

Benchmarking package DEA engine. modelling plotting packages Suggests; function checks ones needs errors informatively missing.

title: Compute DEA multiplier (weight) solutions — compute_multiplier_weights
text: unit \(o\) model maximises weighted output \(u^\top y_o\) subject normalisation \(v^\top x_o = 1\) \(u^\top y_j - v^\top x_j \le 0\) every unit \(j\), \(u, v \ge \epsilon\). optimal value unit's efficiency score. DEA multiplier solutions generally unique: efficient units degenerate vertices admit alternative optimal weight vectors. function returns one optimal solution (vertex solver settles ), canonical one.
